# R1 Digest — Introduction (190–1034)

Source: Longman, NICOT *Song of Songs*, Introduction I–XII (Title through Significance and Theology). Slice: `R1_intro_190-1034.txt`. Bibliography not in range.

## Claims

### C-R1-01 | Title as superlative “best song”
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** The Hebrew title *šîr haššîrîm* (first two words of 1:1) is a construct singular–plural of the same word denoting a superlative: “the best song of all,” analogous to Eccles. 1:2 (“utterly meaningless”), Exod. 29:37 (“Holy of Holies”), Deut. 10:14 (“heaven of heavens”), Gen. 9:25 (“servant of servants”). Origen ranked it best of seven scriptural songs; rabbis ranked it best of the Solomonic corpus; German *Hoheleid* since Luther captures “the best song.”
- **Quote:** "The most obvious meaning of this phrase follows from a recognition that the syntax (the use of the same word in construct relationship, first in the singular and the second time in the plural) denotes a superlative in Hebrew. This, in other words, is the best song of all."
- **Locus:** I. Title
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R1-02 | Title also signals centrifugal/centripetal unity (Song / Songs)
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** Beyond superlative sense, the title also marks structure: centripetal unity (occasional refrain, unity of persona → singular *Song*) and centrifugal independence of poems (→ *Songs*); “something like an erotic psalter.”
- **Quote:** "I believe it intends to convey more than simply \"the best song.\" When we explain the structure of the book, we will see that there are both centrifugal and centripetal forces at work. We will argue that there is a loose unity to the Song suggested by an occasional refrain and a unity of persona (thus the singular Song), but that the poems are ultimately independent of one another. The book is something like an erotic psalter (thus Songs)."
- **Locus:** I. Title
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]]

### C-R1-03 | Alternative titles and canonical placement
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** “Song of Solomon” highlights the superscription’s Solomonic tie but is misleading if it implies full Solomonic authorship. “Canticles” from Vulgate *Canticum canticorum*. In the Hebrew Bible the Song is fourth in the Ketubim; English order follows Ecclesiastes, Hebrew precedes it, yielding Proverbs–Ruth–Song with virtuous/assertive women after Prov. 31:10–31. As one of the Megillot it was read on the eighth day of Passover—association likely from historical-allegorical reading (Exodus → Messiah).
- **Quote:** "Song of Songs is the fourth book in the third section of the Hebrew Bible (the Ketubim). While in the English canon it follows Ecclesiastes, in the Hebrew it precedes it. In the latter, as a result, we have the interesting and surely intentional order of Proverbs, Ruth, and the Song."
- **Locus:** I. Title
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]]

### C-R1-04 | Superscription 1:1 — possible senses of *lešĕlōmōh*
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** The superscription *šîr haššîrîm ʾăšer lišlōmōh* functions like a title page; the subordinate clause’s *le* on Solomon can mean dedicated to, by (authorship), concerning (subject), or “Solomonic” (wisdom literary tradition). Traditionally the book was taken as written by Solomon (if not also about him).
- **Quote:** "The preposition le that is prefixed to Solomon's name can theoretically be understood in more than one way in this context: To Solomon: The book is dedicated to Solomon. By Solomon: Authorship. Concerning Solomon: Solomon is the subject matter of the book. Solomonic: which may mean something like \"in the Solomonic/wisdom literary tradition.\""
- **Locus:** II. Authorship
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]]

### C-R1-05 | Traditional Solomonic authorship and modern defenses
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** Midrash Rabbah places Song–Proverbs–Ecclesiastes in Solomon’s life phases (youth songs → sententious → vanity); Song as youthful composition before apostasy. Modern defenders cite wealth/international-trade imagery (e.g. 4:13–14), natural reading of superscription as authorship, and *lamed* as authorship marker elsewhere; 1 Kgs 4:29–34 records 3000 proverbs and 1005 songs.
- **Quote:** "It seems most natural on the basis of this evidence to conclude that the superscription is making the claim that Solomon wrote the Song in its entirety. For those who believe that the Bible speaks authoritatively in such matters, this seems the end of the discussion. ... However, the situation is not quite so simple. There are significant reasons to question the idea that Solomon wrote the entirety of the Song."
- **Locus:** II. Authorship
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]]

### C-R1-06 | Language not a reliable date/authorship indicator
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** Language does not securely date the book: knowledge of Hebrew development and foreign influence is tenuous; Aramaisms no longer force late dating (Tell Fekheriye, 11th c. B.C.; contact from David, 2 Sam. 8:5–8); one purported Persian loanword (*pardēs*, 4:13) is insufficient; linguistic updating of earlier material is possible, including poetry without demonstrable meter.
- **Quote:** "I simply want to suggest that language is not a reliable indicator of the date of a book for two reasons. First, our knowledge of the development of the Hebrew language is tenuous, particularly in terms of the influence that other languages had on Hebrew. ... Second, we are ignorant concerning the possible linguistic updating of earlier biblical material."
- **Locus:** II. Authorship; cf. IV. Language
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]]

### C-R1-07 | Solomon’s love-life disqualifies him as author of exclusive love poetry
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** The Song extols exclusive, committed love; Solomon’s tradition is many wives/concubines (1 Kgs 11:1ff.), Pharaoh’s daughter valued for alliance not unique love, apostasy via foreign wives, and national calamity/division—making Solomonic authorship of this book unlikely; “pure youth” rabbinic legend is a stretch.
- **Quote:** "Song extols an exclusive, committed relationship. To these lovers there is only one other person - each other. Yet the historical tradition concerning Solomon does not focus on one woman but many wives and concubines. ... All of this is to query the likelihood of a book about romantic love being written by Solomon."
- **Locus:** II. Authorship
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]]

### C-R1-08 | Minimal Solomonic role in the poems; “king”/“shepherd” as epithets
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** Only three passages name Solomon, and there he is object not composer: 1:5 (dark tents—if named at all); 3:6–11 (wedding’s glory promotes marriage institution, not that Solomon married the Song’s woman); 8:11–12 (negative: tries to buy love—unlikely self-portrait). “King” like “shepherd” is epithet of respect/endearment, not political sovereign or Solomon-cipher. “Shulammite” (7:1 ET 6:13) may be feminine of Solomon for etymological “peace.”
- **Quote:** "A mere three passages even mention Solomon at all, and in all three it is clear that Solomon is the object of the poem, not its composer. ... most recent scholarship has rightly recognized that king, like shepherd, is an epithet of respect and endearment, not a reference to an actual political sovereign and certainly not a cipher for Solomon."
- **Locus:** II. Authorship
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]]

### C-R1-09 | Superscription like Proverbs: Solomonic association, not whole-book authorship
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** Parallel to Proverbs (and Qohelet’s fictional Solomonic background for Ecclesiastes): Solomon may have written one or more poems, but nothing indisputably connects the whole anthology to him; the book does not tell a Solomon story (that requires eisegesis). Longman translates the preposition purposively ambiguous: “The Song of Songs, which concerns Solomon.”
- **Quote:** "In our opinion, the lislomoh in the Song of Songs is most like the mention of Solomon in the superscription of the book of Proverbs. ... There is nothing inconceivable about the idea that Solomon wrote one or more of the poems. However, there is also nothing that indisputably connects the book with Solomon. ... Our translation of the preposition in the superscription (The Song of Songs, which concerns Solomon) is purposively ambiguous in terms of Solomon's relationship to the Song."
- **Locus:** II. Authorship
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R1-10 | Female authorship debated; gender of author unknowable
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** Woman’s voice dominates (~61.5/117 verses per Brenner); some argue certain poems are “essentially feminine”; Bekkenkamp/van Dijk link women’s song tradition; Goiten posits a court female singer under Solomon; Landy/LaCocque: female poet resisting norms. Clines counters: ideal male fantasy for erotic male public. Longman: debates reveal more about commentators than the Song; gender of author(s) unknown—collection by men, women, or both.
- **Quote:** "The most honest appraisal is that we do not know for certain who wrote the songs of the Song, a man or a woman, and in any case it is a collection of love poetry, whether by men, or women, or both."
- **Locus:** II. Authorship — A Woman Poet?
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]]

### C-R1-11 | Literary style: Hebrew poetry features
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** The Song has terseness, parallelism, imagery, and secondary devices; one of three poetical books with special Masoretic accents (*teʿamim*). Terseness: short cola (~3 major words), ellipsis (e.g. 8:6a verb omission), sparse conjunctions → intentional ambiguity/emotional richness. Parallelism (Lowth; Kugel “a, what’s more b”): development not mere equivalence; often subtle in the Song (e.g. dew/drizzle; wasf 4:3 metaphor extension); also grammatical/phonological. Imagery densest/most enigmatic in Bible; simile vs metaphor (4:1); all senses; double entendre; Munro’s spheres (courtly, family, nature, space/time) plus military (1:9; 4:4; 6:4, 10). Secondary devices (inclusio, merism, chiasm) treated in commentary.
- **Quote:** "The Song bears all the characteristics of what we recognize as Hebrew poetry: terseness, parallelism, imagery, and secondary poetical devices. ... Indeed, the Song presents us with perhaps the largest concentration of imagery anywhere in the Bible, and its images are also among the most suggestive and, at times, enigmatic."
- **Locus:** III. Literary Style
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]]

### C-R1-12 | Characterization: woman, man, chorus, family
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** No narrator, no overarching plot; consistency of persona. **Woman** dominant, initiates/pursues, modest self-view, magnificent in wasfs; young (marriage early/mid-teens per Fox). **Man** desired and desiring; “king” and “shepherd” figurative roles of respect/desire, not Solomon dual figures. **Daughters of Jerusalem/Zion/young women**: literary device—city girls, naive; functions as sounding board, contrast (city vs country), and students warned not to awaken love early (2:7; 3:5; 8:4). **Brothers** (1:5–6; 8:8–9) = control of sexuality/societal norms; father absent; mother linked to sexuality contexts (3:4, 11; 6:9; 8:1).
- **Quote:** "The Song speaks through its characters. There is no narrator, and we will argue below that there is no overarching narrative or plot. However, the characters whom we hear in the Song have a consistency of persona..."
- **Locus:** III. Literary Style — Characterization
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]]

### C-R1-13 | Language details do not fix date
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** Relative *še* vs *ʾăšer* once thought late but occurs in early texts (Judg. 5:7)—may be dialect/genre. Tamil-influence spice terms (Rabin) and Solomonic India trade are enticing but not exclusive; alternate etymologies (e.g. *kōper* in Ugaritic). Aramaic/Persian/Greek loanword arguments disputed (*bĕrôt*, *nāṭar*, *sĕtāw*; *ʾappiryôn* 3:9; *pardēs* 4:13)—paths of entry uncertain.
- **Quote:** "We can infer nothing about date from the use of the relative pronoun. ... We cannot be certain about the way these words came into the Hebrew language."
- **Locus:** IV. Language
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]]

### C-R1-14 | Date: agnostic; collection may span periods
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** Authorship and language yield agnosticism on date; as anthology like Psalms/Proverbs, poems may derive from different times; some may be Solomonic, others later. With Gordis: lyrical, no historical allusions—“most of the songs are undatable”; timeless quality; nothing at stake for interpretation.
- **Quote:** "Our observations of the language as well as the authorship of the book lead us to an agnostic stand on the issue of date. ... We agree with R. Gordis that \"being lyrical in character, with no historical allusions, most of the songs are undatable.\""
- **Locus:** V. Date
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]]

### C-R1-15 | Text: MT reliable; DSS and versions
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** MT of the Song is without major problems, well supported by versions, basis of Longman’s translation. Difficulties are rare words, rich poetry, and genre—not transmission. Four DSS MSS, Herodian ~30 B.C.–A.D. 70: 4QCantᵃ, 4QCantᵇ substantial; 6QCant not substantial; Abegg/Flint/Ulrich speculation that 4QCantᵃ intentionally omitted erotic 4:7–6:11 is unlikely. LXX, Peshitta, Latin only occasional variants; Aramaic more reception history than text.
- **Quote:** "The Hebrew text (MT) of the Song of Songs is without major problems, is strongly supported by the versions, and is the basis of the following translation and commentary. The difficulties encountered in the text have to do with the unusual number of rare words, the rich poetry, and the genre rather than with any problems with the text's transmission."
- **Locus:** VI. The Text
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]]

### C-R1-16 | History of interpretation: early debate (Aqiba vs banquet use)
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** Rabbi Aqiba (~A.D. 100) forbids singing the Song as a banquet “ditty” and defends canonicity: all ages not worth the day the Song was given; Writings holy, Song “Holy of Holies.” Lines already drawn: erotic surface vs God–humanity meaning. Saadia: interpreters differ because the Song resembles “locks to which the keys have been lost”—genre is the key. Pre-Aqiba evidence scanty; LXX shows no allegory (may be literal translation only). Official community by Aqiba’s time likely had already imposed foreign meaning.
- **Quote:** "Whoever sings the Song of Songs with a tremulous voice in a banquet hall and (so) treats it as a sort of ditty has no share in the world to come. ... It appears that the lines were drawn early over the question whether the surface meaning of the text had to do with human sexuality or the relationship between God and humanity."
- **Locus:** VII. History of Interpretation
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]]

### C-R1-17 | Allegory vs allegorical strategy; Song not itself an allegory
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** Distinguish allegorical literature (author intends surface as continuous symbol—*Pilgrim’s Progress*; Jotham’s trees Judg. 9) from allegorical interpretive strategy. By definition the Song is not an allegory: “no signals that it is to be read in any other way than as a love song.” Yet it was object of allegorical interpretation from earliest recorded commentary. Greek myth allegory (defense of immoral gods) supplied the method.
- **Quote:** "Though allegory does appear in the Hebrew Bible, it is clear from our definition and example that the Song of Songs is not an allegory. The book itself has no signals that it is to be read in any other way than as a love song. No one can dispute this fact. ... Even though the Song is not an allegory as such, it has been the object of an allegorical interpretation from the very beginning of recorded commentary on the book."
- **Locus:** VII — Allegorical Interpretations
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]]

### C-R1-18 | Jewish historical allegories (Targum)
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** Dominant early Jewish allegory: man = God, woman = Israel; surface sensual love displaced. Targum (ca. A.D. 700–900) reads Song as redemptive history Exodus → Messianic age (7:14–8:7) with flashbacks; Song ninth of Ten Songs, “best of them all,” uttered by Holy Spirit. Sample 1:2–9: kisses = Law/Sinai; bedroom = Palestine; blackness = golden calf; etc. Arbitrary: different historical allegories similar but not identical. Loewe: anti-Christian/anti-mystical tendenz in Targum.
- **Quote:** "most Jewish allegorical interpretations begin with the idea that the man in the Song is God and the woman is Israel. The Song of Songs, then, is not about what it seems to be about on the surface, the sensual love between a man and a woman. It is actually about the love that God has for Israel."
- **Locus:** VII — Jewish Allegories — Historical
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]]

### C-R1-19 | Jewish philosophical/mystical allegories
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** Alternative Jewish line: God and individual soul. Early *Shiʿur Qomah* midrash on 5:10–16 lover’s body. Medieval Maimonidean: Gersonides—man = Active Intellect, woman = material intellect; union as highest perfection; daughters of Jerusalem = soul faculties. Abravanel (16th c.): man = Solomon, woman = Wisdom. Notable: remarkable repression of literal/erotic reading except Aqiba’s tavern-singers.
- **Quote:** "Besides those, chided by Aqiba, singing at the taverns, no one affirms a reading of the Song that promotes an erotic understanding of the relationship between the man and the woman."
- **Locus:** VII — Jewish Allegories — Philosophical/Mystical
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]]

### C-R1-20 | Christian allegory: Hippolytus, Origen, Jerome, Bernard
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** Hippolytus (~A.D. 200): e.g. woman’s breasts 4:5 = OT and NT; Christian shift of referents from God/Israel to Jesus/Church (or soul). Origen (185–253/54): knew Song as epithalamium/wedding song on form but spiritualized Bridegroom/Bride = Christ and Church/soul; “desexed” via allegory; Neoplatonist body-denigration; castration tradition; vast commentary; debated rabbis (e.g. Yohanan) on 1:2 wine/breasts. Jerome brought Origen west; delayed Song in Paula’s curriculum until spiritual bridal grasped. Bernard: 86 sermons only through 3:1; for spiritually mature after Eccles./Proverbs; bride = soul, groom = God; letter “outer husk”; Phipps links contempt for flesh/females and violence toward Abelard.
- **Quote:** "Origen certainly understood that the form of the Song had to do with human marriage. ... Yet the \"Bridegroom\" and the \"Bride\" in the Song are immediately spiritualized in Origen's conception of the book; they are identified, respectively, with Jesus Christ and the Church or, at least occasionally, the individual human soul. ... \"these things seem to me to afford no profit to the reader as far as the story goes...\""
- **Locus:** VII — Christian Allegorical Interpretation
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]], [[divine-human-marriage]]

### C-R1-21 | Later Christian allegory: Luther political; Reformed historical; Wesley; modern wane
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** Luther rejects Origen’s and Theodore’s extremes but offers political allegory: Solomon’s government/peace with God, not God–Church. 17th-c. Reformed (Brightman, Cocceius et al.): historical allegory through Reformation/Calvin; Westminster condemned “hot carnal pamphlet.” Wesley: literal application to Solomon/Pharaoh’s daughter “absurd and monstrous.” Academic wane since mid-19th c.; still popular preaching; 20th-c. Catholic exceptions (Feuillet, Robert, Tournay). Keel: agreement among allegorizers usually from copying.
- **Quote:** "The allegorical approach has gone from being the dominant approach to the interpretation to the Song to almost a kind of eccentric archaism."
- **Locus:** VII — Christian Allegorical Interpretation (later)
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]]

### C-R1-22 | Why allegory was rejected (four reasons)
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** Universally recognized 19th-c. genre shift. Reasons: (1) Platonic spiritual-over-physical ethos made allegory a repression strategy once canonicity was fixed; (2) ad hoc arbitrariness—no textual signals; breasts variously Church, testaments, love precepts, Blood/Water, outer/inner man (Gregory of Nyssa)—Enlightenment demand for literary argument; (3) ANE love poems (Egypt, Mesopotamia, Ugarit) clearly human love; (4) modern Middle Eastern wasf/wedding customs (Wetzstein); also new positive appreciation of body/image of God (Gen. 1:27).
- **Quote:** "However, there is absolutely nothing in the Song of Songs itself that hints of a meaning different from the sexual meaning. As a result, the assignment of spiritual meaning to the text assumes an incredibly arbitrary character. ... In the light of these discoveries, it became increasingly difficult to read the Song in a strictly allegorical fashion."
- **Locus:** VII — The Rejection of the Allegorical Approach
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]]

### C-R1-23 | Literal/natural reading and precursors
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** Literal/natural reading resists code-key exegesis; applies normal literary principles; “literal” ≠ flat—affirms rich poetic ambiguity. Precursors: Theodore of Mopsuestia (Solomon–Egyptian princess love poem; thought unfit for Scripture; condemned Constantinople II 553); Castellio (love poem, unworthy of canon) vs Calvin (physical love + belonging in canon; opposed Castellio’s exclusion). Modern standard for intention, but then sub-schools on type of love: drama (2- and 3-character) vs anthology.
- **Quote:** "The literal/natural reading of the Song resists the idea that the Song is a code, saying something different than the words imply. There is no need for a special key to unlock the code, but rather the interpreter applies the same principles to the Song as he or she would to any other comparable writing. ... literal does not mean a flat or plain interpretation."
- **Locus:** VII — The Literal/Natural Interpretation
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]]

### C-R1-24 | Dramatic approach: two-character (Delitzsch)
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** “Dramatic” = plot construction, not necessarily staged theater. Two-character: Solomon + Shulammite (Delitzsch: rustic humble maiden who draws Solomon from polygamy toward Gen. 2 marriage ideal); six acts/two scenes each from mutual affection through covenant ratification. King and shepherd not split.
- **Quote:** "What unites the interpretations that, in spite of their differences, we call the dramatic approach is their construction of a plot. They argue, against the allegorical approach, that the Song is about human love, but they also believe it tells a story."
- **Locus:** VII — The Dramatic Approach — Two Characters
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]]

### C-R1-25 | Dramatic approach: three-character (Ibn Ezra; Provan)
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** Three-character (from Ibn Ezra): separates king from shepherd—love triangle; country girl resists lustful Solomon for shepherd love. Provan’s twist: woman already unhappy in Solomon’s harem; fidelity to first love over legal/royal possession; “superiority of true love over legal love.”
- **Quote:** "the three-character view discovered the third character by separating the king from the shepherd in the book, thus producing a love triangle. ... It is a stirring tale of fidelity to first love in the face of power, coercion and all the temptations of the royal court."
- **Locus:** VII — Three Characters
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]]

### C-R1-26 | Critique of drama; Song as anthology of love poems (23)
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** Drama shares allegory’s fatal flaw: nothing in text supports it—dialogue without stage directions or narrative voice; speaker rubrics not original Hebrew; ~10% of speakers uncertain; overinterpretation (shepherd ≠ king) to force plot. Narrative impulse, not the text, produces drama. Anthology: individual poems of uncertain/doubtful connection; overall coherence without strict plot—“erotic psalter.” Canonical poem-divisions not transmitted; count debated (Landsberger ~every verse; Goulder 14; Falk 31; Longman **23**). Commentary task: metaphors and emotional texture, not story construction.
- **Quote:** "In my opinion, the dramatic approach has the same fatal shortcoming as the allegorical approach. Nothing in the text supports taking this interpretive strategy. ... We thus conclude that the Song is an anthology of love poems, a kind of erotic psalter. ... our analysis below will offer twenty-three."
- **Locus:** VII — Critique of the Dramatic Approach; Love Poetry
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]]

### C-R1-27 | Cultic interpretations rejected (Meek/Kramer; Pope marzeah)
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** Sacred marriage (Dumuzi–Inanna / Tammuz–Ishtar) reflex theory (Meek; Kramer): no support in Song; no OT marriage ritual of this type; monotheism of canon rejects female counterpart. No contemporary support for Meek. Pope’s marzeah (funerary life-over-death meal; climax 8:6c–d): OT mentions marzeah only to castigate (Amos 6:7; Jer. 16:5); never in Song—independent acknowledgments of love’s power over death likelier than genetic link.
- **Quote:** "Nothing in the Song itself supports the idea that it is part of a Hebrew sacred marriage ritual, and, indeed, there is no hint of a marriage ritual anywhere in the Old Testament. ... Thus, it is more likely that both the marzeah and the Song acknowledge the power of love over death independently than that there is some kind of connection between the two."
- **Locus:** VII — Alternative Theories — Cultic
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]]

### C-R1-28 | Psychological (Landy) and political (Stadelmann) rejected
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** Landy: wisdom love poetry + Freudian/Jungian psyche allegory (bisexual mother archetype)—insights without jargon; “learning more about the scholar”; another allegory. Stadelmann: political allegory under Persian domination—Solomon = Davidic state, woman = Judah’s people; needs external “key”; like Luther’s political move; lacks textual warrant; do not avoid obvious sexual meaning.
- **Quote:** "once again we encounter a type of allegory, in this case the allegory of one's psyche, rather than an exposition of the text. ... Stadlemann's analysis suffers the weakness of all allegorical readings: the lack of any indication within the text that we are to read the text in the manner he describes."
- **Locus:** VII — Psychological; Political Interpretation
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]]

### C-R1-29 | Genre: lyric love-poetry anthology; wisdom connection
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** Genre = anthology of lyric love poetry expressing thoughts/feelings via characters to evoke them in readers; closest parallels ANE love poems, not much in HB (Ps. 45 similar but third-person). Poems loosely connected by refrains, persona consistency, repeated themes/metaphors. Reading strategy: unpack metaphors, customs, emotions—not narrative or allegory. Wisdom (Childs, Landy, et al.) additional not replacement: applies God’s will to life’s nitty-gritty; intense exclusive faithful love reveals will for man–woman relationship; Murphy: explication of Prov. 30:19; Munro: young woman instructs chorus; explicit theological language lacking yet canonically rich.
- **Quote:** "We have surveyed the major options and have anticipated our identification of the Song as an anthology of love poetry. More specifically, the Song is lyric poetry that expresses the thoughts and feelings of the poet(s) via the characters of his artistic creation with the intention of evoking those thoughts and feelings in the heart and mind of the reader."
- **Locus:** VIII. Genre
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]]

### C-R1-30 | Forms of individual poems
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** Forms include monologue (2:8–17; 7:12–14) and dialogue (1:15–17; 2:1–7; 4:1–5:1; 8:13–14); admiration songs, descriptions of experience, yearning, invitations, tease (1:7–8), wasf (4:1–7, 12–14; 5:10–16; 6:4–6; 7:2–8).
- **Quote:** "Here we will just list the different forms and give examples in parentheses. First, we see the use of both monologue ... and dialogue. ... Second, in terms of content we have noted admiration songs ... the wasf..."
- **Locus:** VIII. Genre

### C-R1-31 | ANE background: Egyptian love poetry primary parallel
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** Song not in vacuum; ANE parallels support human (not divine) love as primary. Egyptian Ramesside (19th–20th Dyn., 1305–1150 B.C.): Chester Beatty I, Harris 500, Turin, Cairo Love Songs; Fox: entertainment at banquets, not cultic; collection not story; monologues and dual speakers who speak *about* more than *to* each other (unlike Song); lovers as types not historical persons; sister epithet, floral/water imagery, wasf-like descriptions. Mesopotamian (Sumerian three types: divine lovers; king–Inanna; non-royal): similar metaphors but nothing quite like Song; Ludingirra-to-mother letter closest descriptive parallel. Northwest Semitic: no Song equivalent; Kirtu’s Hurriya description snippet. Pre-Islamic Arabic odes (Jinbachian); Tamil (Mariaselvam)—similarities, genetic link doubtful; Egypt closest.
- **Quote:** "In anticipation of this evidence, we argued that the Song speaks primarily of human, not divine, love. The most important evidence comes from Egypt... ... Egyptian love poetry provides a closer parallel."
- **Locus:** IX. Ancient Near Eastern Background
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]]

### C-R1-32 | ANE significance: shared language of love; Song’s teaching edge
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** Parallels show love language crosses borders without direct song-borrowing; elite awareness like foreign wisdom (1 Kgs 4:29–34). Shared: human love/sexuality topic, descriptive poem form, analogous epithets/images. Differences: non-Hebrew examples lack true dialogue (monologue or narrative); Egyptian purpose entertainment; Song may teach chorus by example/admonition about love’s nature and appropriate behavior.
- **Quote:** "the Song shares the same general topic of human love and sexuality, similar forms (notably the \"descriptive poem\"), and analogous epithets and images. ... it is possible to discern in the relationship between the young woman and the chorus in the Song an intention to teach the latter, by example and admonition, the nature of love and its appropriate behavior."
- **Locus:** IX — Significance
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]]

### C-R1-33 | Structure: single Song of many songs; 23 units; refrains; no chiasm schemes
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** Genre drives structure: drama needs plot unity (rejected); anthologists split macrostructure (6–8 poems) vs many independent microstructures. Longman balanced: one Song of many Songs—centripetal (verbal echoes, character consistency, scene repetition, refrains) and centrifugal forces; Cotterell: collection on erotic theme, Solomonic naming, welded by allusion/key vocabulary, no narrative timeline. Flow/progression without strict plot. Chiastic schemes (Exum, Shea, Webster) force unequal units/selective content; analysts disagree—subtle manipulation.
- **Quote:** "It is a single Song composed of many different Songs. ... \"the Song is a collection of songs on a common and generally erotic theme, legitimated by the naming of Solomon, skillfully welded together both by allusion and by the repetition of key vocabulary, but offering no narrative time line maintained through the work\""
- **Locus:** X. Structure
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]]

### C-R1-34 | Canon: “defile the hands,” early inclusion, allegory as product not cause
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** Canonical books self-attesting (Ridderbos) yet external attestation surveyed. Aqiba’s “Holy of Holies” / hands unclean uttered amid dispute (vs R. Yose). Song among handful of contested books; yet well situated early: Aquila, Melito, Tertullian (2nd c.); likely in Josephus’s 22 and 4 Ezra’s 24 (opinion to 2nd c. B.C.). “Defile the hands”: usually = canonicity (holy touch requires cleansing); Broyde alternative: denial of hands-defiling acknowledges absence of Tetragrammaton (with Ecclesiastes, Esther), protecting YHWH-name scrolls from food/rodents—not full rejection. Why included unknown; Christians followed Jews. Solomonic connection or allegory often proposed; Wisdom of Solomon shows Solomonic name insufficient; **allegorization more likely product of canonicity than its cause**.
- **Quote:** "Most scholars, however, conclude that the Song was well situated within the canon as early as we have mention of such matters. ... Many think it is either the connection with Solomon or else the allegorical interpretation of the Song that won the day. However, there are putative Solomonic writings that never made it into the mainstream canon (Wisdom of Solomon), and it is much more likely that the allegorization of the Song was a product of the book's inclusion in the canon rather than vice versa."
- **Locus:** XI. Canon
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]]

### C-R1-35 | Significance: human love/sexuality primary; Bible without Song unthinkable
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** Primary significance is human love and sexuality against history’s impulse to bypass the sensual. Burden of proof on deniers of human-love application. Without Song, Church/synagogue left with spare, almost exclusively negative words on a major human aspect; God addresses whole people (not souls in flesh-husks)—touch, scent, voice, taste, emotion. Church taboos sex; Song affirms and platforms frank talk; rarely preached.
- **Quote:** "it is important to insist on the Song's primary significance in relationship to an important aspect of our humanity: love and sexuality. ... Without the Song, the Church and synagogue would be left with spare and virtually exclusively negative words about an important aspect of our lives. ... ### C-R1-36 | Marriage context within canon; not free love or sex manual
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** Marriage question hard for story-readers (intimacy early; unmarried scene late 8:8–10; rare marriage language). LaCocque’s “free love” rejected. With Childs: wisdom reflection on love within marriage institution; assumes Hebrew family order. Anthology: some poems courtship, some intimacy only appropriate under public commitment—read in whole-canon bounds. Not dating guide/sex manual—“how-to” vs mood-evoking poetry; may free married couples from false proscriptions.

### C-R1-37 | Warning: do not awaken love; power and danger
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** Besides celebration, Song warns of love’s danger (not only illicit sex). 8:6–7: love’s potent force; can yield heartbreak/fainting/sickness (2:5; 5:8); woman thrice warns daughters of Jerusalem not to arouse love before its time (2:7; 3:5; 8:4). Marriage most intimate human relationship; friendship analogies also dual-edged. Against culture’s sex-idolatry (Playboy): sex subordinate to devotion to God; Song ends in yearning not final satisfying embrace—no perfect marriage this side of heaven; speaks to singles (chorus as unmarried women schooled by young woman).
- **Quote:** "In spite of the predominant note of celebration, the Song also issues a warning about the danger of love, and not just illicit sex. ... It is this that leads the woman to warn the \"daughters of Jerusalem\" not to arouse love before its time (2:7; 3:5; 8:4)."

### C-R1-38 | Functional decanonization warning (Carr)
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** David Carr: 19th-c. shift from allegory to literal accompanied “functional decanonization”—recognition of sexual nature led to *less* use in sermons and academic writing. For those holding whole-canon relevance: battle only half-won if true nature recognized but Song unused.
- **Quote:** "David Carr has pointed out that the shift in the nineteenth century from an allegorical to a literal reading was accompanied by what he calls a \"functional decanonization\" of the Song. That is, while the academy and the Church now recognize the sexual nature of the Song, this has led to less actual use of the text in sermons and even academic writing. ... the battle is only half won if, when the text's true nature is recognized, it is not then used."
- **Locus:** XII — As Love Poetry (close)
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R1-39 | Sexuality redeemed: Gen 2–3 → Song as already–not yet healing
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** Shaped by Phyllis Trible: creation of sexual relationship → distortion → redemption. Gen 2: equality/intimacy (rib; Spurgeon via Wenham), naked without shame. Fall: first fracture shows in sexuality (fig leaves); Gen 3:16 *tĕšûqâ* as desire to dominate (Foh; cf. Gen 4:7), mutual power struggle. Song: man and woman in garden, naked without shame (poems incl. 1:15–17; 2:1–7, 8–17; 4:10–5:1; etc.)—echoes Eden; healing of intimacy happens yet incomplete. Egalitarian mutuality; *tĕšûqâ* only again at Song 7:11 ET 7:10 positively in mutual refrain. Still: foxes (2:15); city poems of failed union (3:1–3; 5:2–7); thrice “do not awaken.” Redemption already–not yet; consummation eschatological. Luke 20:27–40: do not impose cold non-sensual heaven; nature of angelic/heavenly relationships open; both divine–human and human–human relationships fully restored then.
- **Quote:** "In the Song of Songs we read about the man and the woman in the garden. They are naked, and feel no shame. ... The implication of a canonical reading of the Song is that the book speaks of the healing of intimacy. Not that that healing is fully accomplished. ... The redemption of our intimate human relationships, indeed like the redemption of our relationships with God, is an already-not yet phenomenon."
- **Locus:** XII — As the Story of Sexuality Redeemed
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]], [[divine-human-marriage]]

### C-R1-40 | Divine–human relationship: legitimate theological reading without allegory’s errors
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** Full circle: after rejecting allegory’s imposed surface-code, affirm theological reading *within canon*—God’s relationship likened to marriage (God husband, people wife; not that God is male; female images exist). Marriage as covenant (Mal 2:14); Hosea, Ezek 16/23, Jeremiah, Isaiah: idolatry as adultery, restoration as remarriage; Exod jealousy/prostitution language; NT Eph 5:21–33 (Christ–Church); Rev marriage of the Lamb. More understanding of marriage → more of God-relationship; only two mutually exclusive human relationships (one spouse, one God)—jealousy proper only there. Allegory erred by (1) suppressing human-love dimension and (2) pressing details arbitrarily for specific theological meanings.
- **Quote:** "The allegorical approach was not wrong in insisting that we read the Song as relevant to our relationship to God. The more we understand about marriage, the more we understand about our relationship with God. ... The allegorical approach erred in two ways, however. First, allegorists suppressed the human love dimension of the Song, and, second, they pressed the details in arbitrary ways in order to elicit specific theological meaning from the text."
- **Locus:** XII — As Illuminating the Divine-Human Relationship
- **Targets:** [[song-of-songs]], [[longman-song-of-songs-nicot]], [[divine-human-marriage]]

### C-R1-41 | Conclusion: three avenues of significance
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** Summary: (1) Affirms love, sex, and—read canonically—marriage; warns of intensity’s dangers. Surface = human sexuality. Canonical avenues: (a) sexuality in creation–fall–redemption of relationships (Gen 2–3; healing promise short of eschaton); (b) divine–human relationship via marriage metaphor—emotional intensity, intimacy, exclusivity—with proper reticence about pressing the analogy.
- **Quote:** "In summary, then, the Song of Songs has a large, but often neglected, contribution to make to the religious community and to society. In the first place, it affirms love, sex, and, if read properly within the context of the canon, marriage. Second, it warns readers that such an intense emotion has its dangers. ... from the Song we learn about the emotional intensity, intimacy, and exclusivity of our relationship with the God of the universe."
- **Locus:** XII — Conclusion

### C-R1-42 | Primary intention: mutual exclusive total beautiful love; types not historical persons
- **Claim (attributed Longman):** Song’s primary intention addresses human love/relationships: love mutual, exclusive, total, beautiful; suppressing this distorts the message. Man and woman are poetic types inviting reader identification—not historical personages.
- **Quote:** "Thus, we believe that the Song's primary intention is to address the issues of human love and relationships. According to the Song, love is mutual, exclusive, total, and beautiful. To ignore or suppress this is to distort the message of the book. The man and the woman of the Song are not historical personages but rather poetic types, and as such the poet invites the readers to identify with them."
